questions.explanation: #11 and #83 rest the case for turning off the stream on the treasury's size and spending rate, not on ZCG's performance, and ask that stripping the treasury and ending other streams be separate proposals. The first option mixes in the broader proposals of #6 and #12, and the second misreads #15, where ebfull calls the NSM the location of least resistance rather than the ideal destination.
options: ZCG's grant record is poor, so its stream should stop in the same vote that ends the coinholder stream and sends every remaining fund to the NSM, with no separate proposals.
The NSM is the best long-term home for the money, so ZCG's stream should go there whatever the size of the treasury, the quality of ZCG's work or the views of its members.
The treasury has outgrown any committee, whatever ZCG's performance, so the stream should stop; stripping the existing treasury and ending other streams belong in separate proposals.
The stream should stop only for a while, until ZCG publishes a restructuring plan, after which it should resume at its current size and carry on as before, treasury untouched.
questions.prompt: Which description fits the case for stopping only ZCG's funding stream as a narrow, separate proposal (#11, #83)?

questions.explanation: #15, replying to #13, says the NSM continues to exist with or without ZCG's stream and that not paying miners was not the goal. The 2031 date is the tempting misreading; #2 itself uses it to argue that funds go to miners in the meantime. Private funding of large projects (#1) was offered as a different argument, not as a reply to this point.
options: The NSM already exists and issuance has to go somewhere anyway, so it was the path of least resistance, avoiding payments to miners was never the aim, and its payout can still change.
Miners will spend their extra rewards on Zcash development, as private investors already fund the ecosystem's biggest projects, so the money still reaches builders.
The NSM does not start paying out until 2031, so no miner benefits from the redirected stream unless a later governance vote chooses to release the reserve.
questions.prompt: Some argued that ending ZCG's stream, or sending it to the NSM, mainly gives more money to miners and less to development (#2, #13). What was the reply?

questions.explanation: #136 asked for evidence behind the claim that coinholder voting has matured, and no post answers it. The others were answered: artkor explains his view in #111, thowar2 says in #118 that Labs publishes only reimbursement-related figures, and artkor declines to give an opinion in #50. An unanswered request is not a refuted claim; it only means nobody supplied the evidence.
options: A question asking why a ZCG member supported a cost-plus retroactive funding model for ventures, given its 20% markup charged to coinholders (#109).
A question asking whether the Zcash Labs team publishes internal statistics such as its treasury, as a way to judge the model (#117).
A request for evidence that coinholder voting has matured: how long it has been used, how many iterations, which teams build on it (#136).
A question asking a ZCG member what they think of converting ZCG into a fiat trust that keeps its value and runs on interest (#49).
questions.prompt: Several posts asked for specific evidence, numbers or explanations. Which of these requests never received a reply in the thread?

questions.explanation: #20 asks ebfull and joshs to confirm they were not among the founders' reward recipients, and #33 repeats the point; no post rebuts it. The treasury-size claim drew replies in #82, #53 and #96, the voting-flaws claim in #52 and #76, and the keep-the-treasury claim in #11. Unanswered only means nobody engaged with the point, not that it is correct.
options: Developers and others pushing coinholder voting have conflicts of interest because Zcash already paid founders very large rewards, a point put to ebfull and joshs by name.
ZCG's treasury is too large for any committee to allocate responsibly, whatever its performance, so its funding stream should stop whatever the verdict on its grant decisions.
Coinholder voting suffers from anonymous, possibly uninformed votes and whale influence, so it is not clearly more accountable than the ZCG committee it would replace.
ZCG's existing treasury should stay with ZCG, converted if need be into a trust, with only new deposits stopped rather than the funds being redirected to the NSM.
questions.prompt: Which of these claims did no participant answer or rebut?

questions.explanation: #112 follows artkor's #111 (ZCG funds things that cannot be monetised) and #114 follows thowar2's #113 (own money, no equity, reimbursed only if coinholders agree). In both they accept Labs only as a complement to ZCG, not a replacement, which rules out the third option, and #118 shows Labs does not publish private financials, which rules out the first.
options: Learning that Zcash Labs publishes its full financials, including its treasury, to coinholders, which settled their worries about transparency and hidden returns.
Being told the model risks the team's own money for no equity and pays out only if coinholders agree, and that ZCG funds non-commercial work the model does not.
Being persuaded that Zcash Labs should replace ZCG as the main funding channel for the work, because its incentives are better aligned with the holders who pay.
questions.prompt: A participant who had objected to Zcash Labs' reimbursement-plus-20% model later said they could support it (#112, #114). What brought that about?

questions.explanation: #18, #52 and #76 argue that holders vote on each grant and that retroactive grants have funded security, infrastructure and bug-bounty work, while ZCAP is insular and pays itself through ZCG. The other options misread the debate: #64 notes that on-chain verifiability does not rule out coordination, #115 says retroactive grants force builders to front costs, and the known-identities point is #64's argument about ZCG's committee.
options: Votes are verifiable on-chain, so any coordination or conflict of interest between large holders is easy to detect and rule out before a grant is paid.
Retroactive grants are paid before the work starts, so builders face no risk and never need outside funding, unlike builders under a committee.
Each decision is made by a small panel with known identities, so criticism can be aimed at specific people who can be questioned directly.
Holders vote on every grant and the work funded (audits, bug bounties, emergency response) has been high-signal, while ZCAP is insular and votes itself money.
questions.prompt: Which is the best argument actually made for ending ZCG while keeping the 12% coinholder-grants stream?

questions.explanation: #137 concedes the critics' structural points (no defined goals, selection bias, no skin in the game) and argues they call for fixing governance and incentives, not abandoning a protocol-level funding tool. The first option is contradicted by #24 and #66, where ZCG's defenders accept the ZSA decision was wrong, and the third inverts #1, which says any five people would face the same problem.
options: ZCG has never funded anything that coinholders opposed, so nothing about its decisions needs to change, only the size of its treasury and the pace of its spending.
The structural problems (no defined goals, a passive inbox, no skin in the game) are real but fixable, so repair governance and incentives and put the capital to work.
Replacing the five current members with different people would solve the problem, because the knowledge problem applies only to this particular panel of five.
questions.prompt: Which is the best argument actually made for restructuring ZCG rather than ending it?

questions.explanation: #27, #32 and #64 argue that anonymous votes, uninformed voters and large holders' influence mean Coinholder deserves the scrutiny ZCG gets, and #31 says to remove both or neither. #64 notes a system being vulnerable is not the same as being abused, but asks for both to be examined, not left unchanged, and #64 presents eliminating both as a thought experiment.
options: Coinholder voting should be abolished at once, because it has been captured by miners and mining companies who outvote everyone else on every grant.
ZCG is beyond criticism, because its five members are publicly known and can be questioned individually, which no voting scheme can match, so it needs no scrutiny.
Both ZCG and the coinholder stream should be left exactly as they are, since neither has been shown to be abused in practice and any change would be disruptive.
Anonymous, possibly uninformed votes and concentrated capital make Coinholder hard to hold accountable, so criticising only ZCG is inconsistent; fix, remove or keep both.
questions.prompt: Which statement fairly describes the view of those who said Coinholder voting deserves the same scrutiny as ZCG (#27, #31, #32, #64)?
